title: The Race of the Dune Buggies
summary: Two cousins build homemade dune buggies for a friendly neighborhood race, learning about friction and gears along the way, and showing good sportsmanship when the race does not go as planned.
poll: Winning a race matters more than being a good sport about losing.

versions.title: The Race of the Dune Buggies
versions.text:
Faisal and Tariq are cousins. They like to build things.

One day, they want to build buggies. A buggy is a small car. It is made of wood.

They work in the garage. They use wood and old wheels. Faisal's buggy is red. Tariq's buggy is blue.

The wheels do not turn. "They stick," says Tariq. Grandpa Saeed has an idea. "Put oil on the wheels," he says. The boys add oil. Now the wheels spin.

They look at a bike chain. It has small wheels. These are called gears. Gears help a bike move.

On race day, friends come to watch. Grandpa Saeed starts the race. Faisal and Tariq race down the street.

Tariq's wheel sticks again. He falls behind. Faisal wins the race! He gets a trophy. Tariq gets a certificate.

Faisal says, "Good race!" Tariq says, "Let's build again next year."

versions.title: The Race of the Dune Buggies
versions.text:
Faisal and Tariq are cousins who live right next door to each other, and they love to build things together.

One Saturday, the two boys decide to build their own dune buggies. A buggy is a small, homemade car built mostly from wood. It rolls along on old bike wheels.

They work together in their grandfather's dusty garage. They use wood planks, rope, and bike wheels they found in a box. Faisal paints his buggy a bright, bold red. Tariq paints his a deep blue.

At first, the wheels on both buggies will not turn well at all. "They keep sticking every time we push," says Tariq. He feels rather upset about the problem. Grandpa Saeed watches them work. He has an idea. "Try putting a little oil on the wheels," he says. "That should help them spin much more easily." The boys carefully add oil to each wheel. Soon the wheels spin far more smoothly than before.

They also study an old bike chain kept in a drawer. It has small, round wheels called gears. Gears help a bike move forward using much less effort from the person riding it.

On race day, many neighbors come out to watch the fun. Grandpa Saeed stands proudly at the starting line. He waves a small flag. Faisal and Tariq race their colorful buggies down the long street together.

Partway through the race, Tariq's wheel suddenly sticks again. He slowly falls behind his cousin. Faisal pushes forward and crosses the finish line first, winning the whole race! He proudly gets a shiny gold trophy. Tariq gets a certificate for his strong effort and good sportsmanship.

Faisal grins widely and says, "That was a great race, Tariq!" Tariq laughs warmly and says, "Let's build an even better buggy next year."

versions.title: The Race of the Dune Buggies
versions.text:
Faisal and Tariq are cousins who live right next door to each other. They love building things together almost every weekend.

One Saturday, the two boys decide to build their own dune buggies for the neighborhood race. A buggy, they explain to their little sister, is a small, homemade car built mostly from wood. It rolls along on old bicycle wheels.

They work together in their grandfather's dusty garage. They use wood planks, rope for steering, and bicycle wheels they found in an old box. Faisal paints his buggy a bright, bold red. Tariq paints his a deep blue. Both boys feel proud of their work.

At first, the wheels on both buggies will not turn well. "They keep sticking every time we push," complains Tariq. He feels rather upset by the stubborn problem. Grandpa Saeed watches the boys struggle. He explains that friction between dry parts makes the wheels stick. He suggests they adjust each wheel by adding a little oil. The boys carefully oil each wheel. Soon the wheels spin far more smoothly than before.

They also study an old bicycle chain that Grandpa Saeed keeps in a drawer. It has small, round wheels called gears, all connected by the chain. Gears, he explains, help a bicycle move forward using much less effort from the person pedaling it.

On race day, many neighbors gather along the street to watch the fun. Grandpa Saeed stands proudly at the starting line. He waves a small flag to begin the race. Faisal and Tariq race their colorful buggies down the long street, with everyone cheering loudly.

Partway through the race, Tariq's wheel suddenly sticks again, since he forgot to oil that one wheel. He slowly falls behind his determined cousin. Faisal pushes forward with real effort and crosses the finish line first, winning the whole race! He proudly receives a shiny gold trophy. Tariq receives a certificate for his strong effort and good sportsmanship.

Faisal grins and says, "That was a great race, Tariq!" Tariq laughs warmly and says, "Let's work together and build an even better buggy next year."

versions.title: The Race of the Dune Buggies
versions.text:
Faisal and Tariq are cousins who live right next door to each other. They love building things together almost every single weekend, especially anything with wheels and wood.

One Saturday afternoon, the two boys decide to build their own dune buggies for the upcoming neighborhood race. A buggy, they explain to their curious little sister, is a small, homemade car built mostly from wood. It is steered with a simple length of rope.

They work together in their grandfather's dusty garage. They use wood planks, rope for steering, and bicycle wheels they found tucked away in an old box. Faisal paints his buggy a bright, bold red. Tariq paints his a deep blue, and both boys feel genuinely proud of their work.

At first, however, the wheels on both buggies will not turn well at all. "They keep sticking every single time we push," complains Tariq. He feels rather upset by the stubborn, squeaky problem. Grandpa Saeed watches the boys struggle. He explains that friction between the dry metal parts makes the wheels stick and slows everything down. He suggests they adjust each wheel with a little oil. The boys carefully oil each squeaky wheel. Soon the wheels spin far more smoothly than they had before.

They also spend some time studying an old bicycle chain that Grandpa Saeed keeps in a drawer of his workbench. It has small, round wheels called gears, all connected by the chain. Gears, he patiently explains, help a bicycle move forward using much less effort from the person pedaling it.

On race day, many neighbors gather eagerly along the street to watch the fun. Grandpa Saeed stands proudly at the starting line. He waves a small flag to officially begin the race. Faisal and Tariq race their colorful buggies down the long street, with everyone cheering loudly from the sidelines.

Partway through the race, Tariq's wheel suddenly sticks again, since he completely forgot to oil that one wheel. He slowly falls behind his determined cousin. Faisal pushes forward with real effort and crosses the finish line first, winning the whole race! He proudly receives a shiny gold trophy for first place. Tariq receives a certificate honoring his strong effort and good sportsmanship.

Faisal grins widely and says, "That was a great race, Tariq!" Tariq laughs warmly and says, "Let's work together and build an even better buggy next year."

Faisal and Tariq, cousins who lived right next door to each other, loved building things together almost every weekend, and it would not take you long to notice they especially enjoyed anything with wheels and wood.

One Saturday afternoon, the two boys decided to build their own dune buggies for the upcoming neighborhood race, and they could hardly wait to get started. A buggy, they explained to their little sister, is a small, homemade car built mostly from wood, steered with a simple length of rope.

They worked in their grandfather's dusty garage, using wood planks, rope for steering, and bicycle wheels they had found in an old box. Faisal painted his buggy a bright red. Tariq painted his a deep blue, and both boys felt proud of what they had made together.

At first, the wheels on both buggies simply would not turn well. "They keep sticking every time we push them," complained Tariq, feeling rather upset by the stubborn problem. Grandpa Saeed watched the boys struggle and suggested they adjust each wheel with a little oil, since friction between the dry metal parts makes wheels stick and slows things down. The boys carefully oiled each wheel, and soon the wheels spun far more easily than before.

They also studied an old bicycle chain that their grandfather kept in a drawer. It had small, round wheels called gears, all connected by the chain, and gears, he explained, help a bicycle move forward using much less effort from the rider.

Faisal pushed forward and crossed the finish line first, winning the race. He proudly received a shiny gold trophy, while Tariq received a certificate honoring his strong effort and good sportsmanship despite the setback.

Faisal grinned and said, "That was a great race, Tariq!" Tariq laughed and replied that next year they should work together and build an even better buggy than the ones they had raced that day.

Partway through the race, Tariq's wheel suddenly stuck again, since he had forgotten to oil that one wheel that morning in his excitement, and he slowly began falling behind his determined cousin. Faisal pushed forward and crossed the finish line first, winning the race. versions.title: The Race of the Dune Buggies
versions.text:
Faisal and Tariq, cousins who lived right next door to each other, loved building things together nearly every weekend, a shared enthusiasm that extended to anything involving wheels, wood, and tools.

One sweltering Saturday afternoon, the two cousins decided to build their own dune buggies for the upcoming neighborhood race. They gathered wooden planks, sturdy rope for steering, and bicycle wheels found in an old storage box in a corner of the garage.

Faisal painted his buggy a bold red, while Tariq chose a deep blue. Both boys felt proud of what their own hard work and ingenuity had produced. Yet the wheels on both buggies initially refused to turn smoothly, sticking stubbornly with every push.

Grandfather Saeed, noticing their frustration, explained that friction between dry metal parts was slowing the wheels, and he suggested applying oil to each axle. Once the boys oiled every wheel, the buggies suddenly glided forward with remarkable ease and new momentum.

The cousins also examined an old bicycle chain from Grandfather Saeed's workbench, discovering the small gears connected along its length. Gears, their grandfather explained, form a simple mechanism that lets a bicycle move forward using less effort from the person pedaling.

On race day, nearly the entire neighborhood gathered along the dusty street, eager to watch the cousins compete. Grandfather Saeed stood at the starting line and waved a small checkered flag, beginning the long-awaited race.

Partway through, Tariq's front wheel suddenly stuck fast, since he had forgotten to oil that axle that morning, and he began falling behind his cousin. Faisal, demonstrating genuine perseverance, pushed forward with growing velocity and crossed the finish line first, winning the race outright.

He proudly received a shiny golden trophy for his victory, while Tariq received a certificate honoring his effort and admirable sportsmanship. Faisal praised his cousin's effort, and Tariq, smiling despite his disappointment, congratulated Faisal on a well-earned win, already looking forward to building an even better buggy together next year.

questions.stem: Why does Grandfather Saeed suggest adding oil to the axles?
options: To make the buggy look shinier
To help the wheels turn more easily
To make the buggy heavier
To change the color of the wheels
questions.why: Oil reduces the friction between the dry parts, so the wheels can turn more easily.

wrong.A: Oil is not added for shine.
wrong.C: Oil does not add weight to the buggy.
wrong.D: Oil does not change the wheel's color.

questions.stem: What can you tell about Faisal from how he treats Tariq after winning?
options: He is a poor sport who brags about winning
He is kind and praises his cousin's effort
He refuses to race with Tariq again
He gives his trophy to Tariq
questions.why: Faisal kindly praises Tariq's effort instead of bragging, showing good sportsmanship.

wrong.A: Faisal does not brag; he praises Tariq.
wrong.C: The cousins plan to build together again next year.
wrong.D: Faisal keeps his own trophy.

questions.stem: Why does the author end the story with the cousins planning to build together next year?
options: To show that their friendship matters more than who won
To explain how to build a new buggy
To describe Grandfather Saeed's garage
To carefully list every single official rule of the big race
questions.why: Ending on their shared plans shows that their cousin bond matters more than the win itself.

wrong.B: The ending does not give building steps.
wrong.C: The ending is not about the garage.
wrong.D: The ending does not list race rules.

LOW.prompt: Would you rather win a race alone or race together with a family member like Faisal and Tariq? Explain your answer using at least two details from the story.
checklist: I clearly said what I think.
I used at least two details from the story.
I wrote complete sentences with capital letters and periods.
LOW.modelAnswer: I would rather race together with a family member, like Faisal and Tariq did. They had fun building their buggies together in the garage, and even after Faisal won, they stayed kind to each other. Tariq congratulated Faisal instead of being upset, and they are already planning to build a better buggy together next year.

keyWords.definition: a force that slows things down when two surfaces rub together
keyWords.example: Friction between the tires and the road helps a car stop.

keyWords.definition: connected wheels with teeth that change how much force is needed to move something
keyWords.example: The cyclist shifted gears to climb the steep hill more easily.

keyWords.definition: having a strong will to keep trying and not give up
keyWords.example: The determined runner kept going even though her legs were tired.

keyWords.definition: to change something slightly to make it work better
keyWords.example: We had to adjust the tent poles before the tent would stand up straight.

keyWords.definition: fair and kind behavior when playing or competing in a game
keyWords.example: Shaking hands after a hard loss is a sign of good sportsmanship.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the central idea of the story?
options: Two cousins build buggies and show good sportsmanship during their race.
A grandfather teaches his grandsons how to paint a garage.
Two cousins argue over who owns an old bicycle chain.
A neighborhood committee decides to stop holding races permanently every year.
questions.why: The story follows Faisal and Tariq as they build buggies, solve a friction problem, learn about gears, and show sportsmanship after the race.

wrong.B: Painting the garage is not part of the story.
wrong.C: The cousins do not argue over the chain; they study it together.
wrong.D: The neighborhood race still happens in the story.

questions.stem: What problem do the cousins first notice with their buggies?
options: The buggies are too small to sit in
The wheels will not turn well
The paint will not dry
The rope keeps breaking
questions.why: The cousins notice that the wheels keep sticking and will not turn well because of friction.

wrong.A: Size is not mentioned as a problem.
wrong.C: Drying paint is not an issue in the story.
wrong.D: The story does not mention the rope breaking.

questions.stem: What does Grandfather Saeed do to help solve the sticking-wheel problem?
options: He buys the boys a brand-new buggy from the store downtown
He tells the boys to stop building
He suggests oiling the axles to reduce friction
He enters the race himself
questions.why: Grandfather Saeed explains that friction is the problem and suggests oiling the axles.

wrong.A: He does not buy them a new buggy.
wrong.B: He encourages them, rather than telling them to stop.
wrong.D: Grandfather Saeed does not race in the story.

questions.stem: Why does Tariq most likely fall behind during the race?
options: He secretly decides to let his cousin Faisal win the race on purpose
He takes a longer path than Faisal
He stops to fix his cousin's buggy
His unoiled axle creates friction that slows his wheel
questions.why: Tariq forgot to oil one axle, so friction makes that wheel stick and slows him down.

wrong.A: Tariq is not letting Faisal win on purpose.
wrong.B: Both cousins race the same street.
wrong.C: Tariq does not stop to fix Faisal's buggy.

questions.stem: In the story, the word gears means —
options: small wheels that help a machine move with less effort
a kind of paint used on wooden buggies
a special wrench-like tool used only to oil a bicycle axle
a type of rope used for steering
questions.why: The story explains that gears are the small connected wheels that let a bicycle move using less effort.

wrong.B: Gears are not a kind of paint.
wrong.C: An oil can, not a gear, is used to oil an axle.
wrong.D: Rope, not gears, is used for steering.

questions.stem: Why does Faisal most likely praise Tariq's effort after winning?
options: He feels sorry for his cousin and wants to apologize
He values good sportsmanship more than simply bragging about winning
He is secretly trying to trick his cousin Tariq into racing him again soon
He wants Grandfather Saeed to give him a second trophy
questions.why: Faisal's kind words show that he values friendship and sportsmanship rather than just the win itself.

wrong.A: Faisal has nothing to apologize for; he races fairly.
wrong.C: There is no trick involved in Faisal's kindness.
wrong.D: Faisal is not seeking a second trophy.

questions.stem: What causes the buggies to move more smoothly after the boys work on them?
options: Painting the buggies makes them lighter
Removing the gears makes them faster
Adding oil reduces the friction between the wheels and axles
Adding a lot more rope to the steering makes it much easier to turn
questions.why: Oil reduces friction between the dry metal parts, letting the wheels turn more smoothly.

wrong.A: Paint does not change how much the buggies weigh.
wrong.B: The gears belong to the bicycle chain, not the buggies.
wrong.D: Rope affects steering, not how smoothly the wheels turn.

questions.stem: How does the author organize the events of the story?
options: By comparing different kinds of bicycles in each separate paragraph of the story
By listing facts about neighborhood races in general
By describing Grandfather Saeed's entire life story
By telling events in order: building, fixing friction, racing, then the ending
questions.why: The story follows a clear sequence: building the buggies, fixing the sticking wheels, racing, and the friendly ending.

wrong.A: The story does not compare types of bicycles.
wrong.B: The story is a narrative, not a list of general facts.
wrong.C: Grandfather Saeed's life story is not described.

MID.prompt: Explain how friction affected the cousins' buggies, and how they solved the problem. Use at least two details from the story.
checklist: I explained how friction affected the buggies.
I used at least two details from the story.
I organized my ideas in a clear order.
MID.modelAnswer: Friction made it hard for the cousins' buggies to move at first, because the dry metal wheels and axles rubbed against each other and stuck. Grandfather Saeed noticed the problem and suggested putting oil on the axles. Once the boys oiled each wheel, the friction was reduced, and the buggies rolled much more smoothly. This fix worked well until Tariq forgot to oil one axle again on race day, which slowed him down during the actual race.

keyWords.definition: the force that keeps a moving object going
keyWords.example: The sled gained momentum as it raced down the snowy hill.

keyWords.definition: a set of connected parts that work together inside a machine
keyWords.example: The clock's mechanism includes many small, interlocking gears.

keyWords.definition: cleverness and skill in solving problems or inventing things
keyWords.example: The engineers used great ingenuity to fix the broken bridge quickly.

keyWords.definition: steady effort to keep trying despite difficulty
keyWords.example: It took real perseverance for the climbers to reach the summit.

keyWords.definition: the speed of something moving in a particular direction
keyWords.example: The race car reached a high velocity on the long, straight track.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the story?
options: A neighborhood race is canceled because of bad weather.
A grandfather forbids his grandsons from using tools in the garage.
Two cousins use ingenuity and sportsmanship to build and race buggies.
Two cousins refuse to speak to each other after losing a race.
questions.why: The story highlights the cousins' creative building, their perseverance through the friction problem, and their sportsmanship at the finish.

wrong.A: The race happens as planned; it is not canceled.
wrong.B: Grandfather Saeed encourages their project rather than forbidding it.
wrong.D: The cousins remain close and friendly after the race.

questions.stem: Why does the author include the detail that Grandfather Saeed explains friction to the boys before the race?
options: To explain why the trophy is made of gold
To show that Grandfather Saeed dislikes the boys' project
To suggest that the race will be canceled
To foreshadow that friction will cause trouble again
questions.why: Explaining friction early prepares the reader for Tariq's unoiled axle causing trouble again during the actual race.

wrong.A: The trophy's material is not connected to this explanation.
wrong.B: Grandfather Saeed clearly supports and helps with their project.
wrong.C: The race is not canceled in the story.

questions.stem: How does oiling the axles most directly affect the buggies' performance?
options: It reduces friction, helping the wheels keep their momentum
It makes the buggies heavier and therefore slower
It changes the color of the paint on the wheels
It increases the number of gears on each buggy
questions.why: Reducing friction lets the wheels keep turning with less resistance, helping the buggies maintain momentum.

wrong.B: Oil does not add meaningful weight to the buggies.
wrong.C: Oil does not affect paint color.
wrong.D: Gears belong to the bicycle chain, not the buggies themselves.

questions.stem: In the story, the word ingenuity means —
options: a strong, unpleasant smell
cleverness in solving problems or inventing things
a type of competition prize
the physical force that keeps a moving object in motion over time
questions.why: The cousins' ingenuity is shown through their clever homemade solutions, like using oil to fix friction and repurposing old parts.

wrong.A: Ingenuity has nothing to do with smell.
wrong.C: A trophy, not ingenuity, is the prize.
wrong.D: Momentum, not ingenuity, describes a moving force.

questions.stem: What can readers infer about Faisal's character from his behavior after winning the race?
options: He secretly feels guilty for winning unfairly
He plans to stop building buggies with Tariq
He values sportsmanship more than simply claiming victory
He believes Tariq's mechanical problem was intentional
questions.why: Faisal's generous praise of Tariq shows that he cares about their relationship, not just about winning.

wrong.A: Faisal wins fairly; there is no reason for guilt.
wrong.B: The cousins plan to build together again next year.
wrong.D: Nothing suggests Faisal thinks the problem was intentional.

questions.stem: In what order do these events occur in the story?
options: The race begins, the cousins oil the axles, and they study the bicycle gears
Tariq wins the race, Faisal studies the gears, and the cousins build new buggies
Grandfather Saeed awards the trophy, the cousins build the buggies, and the race begins afterward
They build the buggies, oil the axles, race each other, and then Tariq's wheel sticks again
questions.why: The cousins first build the buggies, then solve the friction problem by oiling the axles, and only during the actual race does Tariq's axle stick again.

wrong.A: The axles are oiled before the race, not after it begins.
wrong.B: Faisal wins the race, not Tariq.
wrong.C: The trophy is awarded after the race, not before the buggies are built.

questions.stem: Why does the author mention that Tariq's wheel sticks again during the race, after it had already been fixed earlier?
options: To show Tariq simply forgot to oil the axle again, a realistic mistake
To suggest that oil never actually solves a friction problem
To imply that Faisal secretly damaged Tariq's buggy
To show that gears, not friction, caused the second problem
questions.why: The story clearly states Tariq forgot to oil that one axle that morning, making the repeated problem realistic rather than mysterious.

wrong.B: Oil clearly worked earlier in the story, improving both buggies.
wrong.C: Nothing suggests Faisal sabotaged his cousin's buggy.
wrong.D: The second problem is caused by friction, not by the gears.

questions.stem: Based on the story, what most likely allows Faisal to win the race despite both cousins starting with similar buggies?
options: Faisal's buggy was simply built from better materials than Tariq's
Tariq's unoiled axle created friction that slowed his momentum
Faisal cheated by taking a shorter path down the street
Grandfather Saeed secretly helped push Faisal's buggy forward
questions.why: Both buggies were built similarly, but Tariq's forgotten, unoiled axle created friction that cost him speed during the race.

wrong.A: Both buggies are built from similar scrap materials.
wrong.C: There is no mention of Faisal taking a shortcut.
wrong.D: Grandfather Saeed only starts the race; he does not push either buggy.

HIGH.prompt: Do you think the race was fair, even though Tariq's wheel got stuck again? Support your argument with evidence from the story, and address a reason someone might disagree with you.
checklist: I supported my position with specific evidence from the story.
I addressed at least one point someone might make against my view.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I think the race was fair, even though Tariq's wheel got stuck again. Both cousins built similar buggies from the same kinds of scrap materials, and both had already learned how to fix the friction problem by oiling their axles. Tariq's second problem happened simply because he forgot to oil that one axle that morning, not because of anything Faisal did. Someone might argue that the race was unlucky for Tariq and therefore not a true test of skill, and that is a fair point to raise. However, since both cousins had an equal chance to prepare carefully, and Faisal's win came from genuine perseverance rather than any unfair advantage, the outcome still reflects a fair and honestly run competition.
